Compactness and complex-line positivity

Reconstructed by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Earlier edition by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI). Original exposition: CC0. Linked programme prerequisites retain their stated licences. Self-checked by the writing AI.

Subharmonic limits are controlled by their integrals and their upper values. Complex-line positivity gives an additional monotonicity: the normalized Laplacian mass of a ball increases with its radius. We prove these facts, identify the density of a holomorphic zero, and compute two families whose curvature lies on algebraic cuts.

The exact inputs are Positive derivatives and canonical representatives, Theorems 3.1–3.2, Corollary 3.3 and Lemma 2.1; Order, positivity and distributional limits, Corollary 3.3 and Theorems 4.1, 5.1–5.2; Convolution as addition of supports, B1–B3 and Proposition 5.1; Boundary flux and weak identities, Theorem 2.1 and Corollaries 2.2–2.4; and Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2. The polydisk proof and Lemma 3.1 of Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones supply convergent holomorphic power series and the identity principle. Their supplied scalar, finite-algebra, integration and angular foundations provide compactness, cutoffs, Fubini, linear changes of variables and sphere measure. Every additional argument is given below.

Subharmonic means the canonical upper semicontinuous function with values in , satisfying the sphere submean inequality and not identically minus infinity on any component. Means use probability measure. We use . An assertion on a closed ball always requires that entire ball to lie in the open domain.

Curvature on complex lines

Write , and set For a real distribution and , define Conjugation and interchange of show that it is real. For smooth , two applications of the chain rule give

An upper semicontinuous , open, is plurisubharmonic when its restriction to each complex affine line is subharmonic or identically minus infinity on each component of the line intersection. It is proper if no ambient component has the latter behavior. Thus properness permits a line contained in the minus-infinity set, as for .

Theorem 1.1 (the Levi criterion). Proper plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable and real subharmonic in dimension . Their distributions satisfy for every . Conversely, a real distribution with all these positive Levi forms has exactly one proper plurisubharmonic representative. Its averages with any fixed nonnegative smooth radial unit-mass profile supported in the unit ball decrease to that representative as the radius decreases to zero.

Proof. Suppose first that has the line property, and fix a closed ball with center and radius inside . Upper semicontinuity gives a finite upper bound there. For a complex unit vector , This includes a line component with value minus infinity. Average over on the real unit sphere. The map is orthogonal, so it preserves sphere measure by the surface-invariance proof preceding U023 Lemma 2.1. Tonelli applied to justifies both orders even if an integral is infinite. The double mean is the real sphere mean. Thus satisfies the real submean inequality. Properness and U023 Theorem 3.2 now give local integrability and real subharmonicity.

For a nonnegative smooth mollifier, is smooth on . Integrate (1.4) on translated disks against the mollifier. The product integral of the absolute value is finite: bound the translation density by , integrate on one compact neighborhood containing every translated circle, and then integrate over the finite angle interval. Fubini proves the line submean inequality for . The two-dimensional Taylor mean formula U023 (3.9) and (1.3) give . Local distributional convergence passes this positivity to .

Conversely the trace in (1.3) gives . U023 supplies a proper real subharmonic representative and radial smoothings decreasing pointwise to it. Each is the positive distribution applied to a nonnegative translated test, hence is nonnegative. Equation (1.3) and U023 in dimension two make the smooth line restrictions subharmonic.

Fix a compact line disk. For all sufficiently small radii the smoothings are defined on a neighborhood of it and bounded above by one earlier smoothing on that compact set. Subtract from this bound and use monotone convergence on its boundary circle. The circle inequalities pass to , including minus-infinity values. The restriction is upper semicontinuous. On a connected line component, either it is everywhere minus infinity or it has a finite point, so U023 Theorem 3.2 applies. It is therefore plurisubharmonic. Any other proper representative is real subharmonic by the first argument; uniqueness in U023 identifies it everywhere. Radial recovery is exactly U023 Corollary 3.3.

Proposition 1.2 (finite maxima and decreasing limits). A finite maximum of proper plurisubharmonic functions is proper plurisubharmonic. The limit of a decreasing sequence of plurisubharmonic functions is, on each ambient component, either proper plurisubharmonic or identically minus infinity.

Proof. A finite maximum is upper semicontinuous. At a finite center value, select a summand attaining it; its circle mean is at most that of the maximum. At a minus-infinity center the inequality is automatic. If a line restriction has a finite point, the two-dimensional converse submean theorem makes it subharmonic throughout that component. In the ambient space the maximum is finite almost everywhere, since its finitely many summands are locally integrable. It is proper.

A decreasing limit is upper semicontinuous: its strict sublevel set is the union of those of the terms. On each compact disk a common finite upper bound is supplied by the first term. Monotone convergence of its differences from that bound passes every circle inequality to the limit. The line restriction is subharmonic or identically minus infinity as above. On an ambient component with a finite point, averaging over directions gives the real submean inequality and U023 propagates integrability throughout that component.

A smooth real convex function has nonnegative second derivatives along both real directions of every complex line, and hence is plurisubharmonic. The converse fails: has zero Levi form but negative second derivative in the direction.

Lemma 2.2 (a bounded family of integrals has a subsequential distributional limit). If real have uniformly bounded norms on every compact subset, a subsequence converges distributionally to a real order-zero distribution.

Proof. Use the compact exhaustion from the integration foundations to choose open relatively compact with and union . We first construct a countable uniformly dense family of smooth tests, allowing approximation of functions supported in by tests supported in .

Extend such a continuous function by zero. On the grid , , use the continuous hats They sum to one, since in each coordinate at most two adjacent hats are nonzero and sum to one. The interpolant with vertex values differs uniformly from by at most its modulus of continuity at . Only finitely many vertex values are nonzero. Replace them by rational real values, adding an arbitrarily small error. All finite rational arrays over these grids form a countable set.

Choose a fixed smooth cutoff on , supported in . Multiplication by , chosen between zero and one, preserves the error bound. Convolve with a fixed smooth bump at rational positive radii smaller than the distance of its support from . The resulting tests stay in and approximate uniformly by uniform continuity. These choices form a countable family; real functions suffice, since complex tests split into real and imaginary parts.

Pairings with every test in the union over are bounded. Bolzano–Weierstrass followed by successive subsequence selection and a diagonal choice gives convergence of all these countably many pairings. For an arbitrary smooth supported in , use the constructed approximants : Thus the selected pairings are Cauchy for every . Their limit is linear, real on real tests, and has a common order-zero bound on each compact support. The distribution criterion of U008 makes it a distribution; its Corollary 3.3 identifies it with a signed Radon measure if desired.

Theorem 2.3 (compactness or collapse). On a connected real open set , a sequence of subharmonic functions with a common upper bound on each compact either tends uniformly to minus infinity on every compact, or has an -convergent subsequence with subharmonic limit. For proper plurisubharmonic functions the limit in the second alternative is plurisubharmonic.

Proof. Failure of uniform collapse gives a subsequence, a compact , points , and a real such that . Take a further subsequence with . Choose . Eventually . If is the common upper bound on the latter closed ball, ball submean gives The right side is bounded below and the positive parts have a uniform bound. Hence the negative parts, and the norms, are uniformly bounded on this first ball. The discarded finitely many terms cause no difficulty.

Here is the propagation step. Suppose a ball has a uniform bound . Suppose and contains a ball of positive volume. For each some finite-valued satisfies ; otherwise its negative integral on exceeds . The ball covers and lies in . The same submean and upper-bound calculation as (2.6) gives a uniform bound on .

Any two points of can be joined by a polygonal path: the set reachable from a fixed point is open, and its complement is open, by inserting short segments in small balls. Connectedness makes it all of . A compact path has a positive distance from the complement. Choose below that distance and the radius of the initial bounded ball, then so that is still below that distance. Partition the path parameter finely enough that consecutive centers are less than apart. At each step lies in the preceding radius- ball, so it contains the required positive-volume . The bound propagates along this finite chain. This reaches a neighborhood of every point. Finitely many such neighborhoods cover each compact set.

Lemma 2.2 now gives a distributional subsequential limit and Theorem 2.1 gives the claimed limit. Levi positivity passes to that distribution in the complex case. Uniform collapse cannot also hold on this subsequence: on a compact ball of positive volume it would force its integral to minus infinity, contradicting a finite limit.

Holomorphic logarithms are stable in integrals

Lemma 3.1 (holomorphic zero sets are null). A holomorphic function which is not identically zero on any component of an open subset of has a zero set of real Lebesgue measure zero.

Proof. In one variable, its first nonzero Taylor coefficient makes each zero isolated. Choose for each zero a rational-center, rational-radius disk which contains it and no other zero. Distinct zeros require distinct disks, so the zero set is at most countable and has area zero.

Induct on . On a polydisk, translating its first center to zero, the polydisk Cauchy formula gives Each coefficient is holomorphic in : it is the first-variable circle integral of , and the locally uniformly convergent differentiated polydisk series from U015 permits differentiation under that compact integral. At least one coefficient is not identically zero on the parameter polydisk. Otherwise vanishes on the whole polydisk and then on its ambient component by the identity principle.

By induction the zero set of this coefficient is null in parameter space. Outside it the one-variable function has a null zero set. Fubini on bounded polydisks, including the exceptional null set times the finite-area first disk, gives zero total volume. A countable polydisk cover exists from the rational Euclidean basis, so the full zero set is null.

Proof. Upper semicontinuity follows from continuity of and the increasing logarithm, including its limit at zero. On any line the holomorphic restriction is identically zero on a component or has isolated finite-order zeros. In the latter case, near a zero , factor , . U020 Corollary 1.2 proves local integrability and (3.2), including a local logarithm for whose real part is harmonic. The pointwise function is the positive potential plus that harmonic function. U023 identifies it as the canonical subharmonic representative at every point, including . Off the zeros it is harmonic. Thus it has the line property. The assumption supplies a finite point on each ambient component, and Theorem 1.1 supplies ambient integrability.

Proof. First work on a connected relatively compact open neighborhood . The identity principle supplies with . Eventually , so those are not identically zero on . Proposition 3.2 applies. Their logarithms have common local upper bounds from local uniform convergence, and their values at have a finite lower bound. Consequently collapse is impossible for every subsequence. At almost every point of , by Lemma 3.1, and there. The summable-error argument in Theorem 2.1 gives almost-everywhere convergence along a further subsequence of any -convergent subsequence. Its limit is therefore . If convergence of the whole sequence failed on a compact in , select a subsequence with errors bounded below by some . The further subsequence just obtained contradicts that bound. Finally cover by finitely many connected relatively compact neighborhoods and take the largest exceptional index. This also handles infinitely many ambient components.

A monotone measure of logarithmic curvature

For proper plurisubharmonic and its positive measure , define For , the distance is infinite. Balls here are open, so boundary mass is excluded. The small-radius limit is called the Lelong number with this normalization.

We will use the following consequence of U008 Theorem 5.2. If positive measures converge distributionally to , then they converge on each ball whose closed ball is interior and whose boundary has zero -mass. To prove it, put all cutoffs in a slightly larger compact ball. A smooth function equal to one there bounds every mass by its convergent pairings. Continuous radial cutoffs which equal one on and zero outside bound from below. Cutoffs equal to one on and zero outside bound it from above. Pass to the continuous-test limits, then let . Continuity from below and above gives and , equal by the boundary assumption. This proves the squeeze without assuming convergence on all Borel sets.

Theorem 4.1 (density monotonicity). The function is nonnegative and increasing. Its limit at zero exists and is finite.

Proof. Translate to zero. For smooth , let be its real sphere mean. For a complex unit vector , let be the circle mean of . Planar flux and (1.3) give This is nonnegative and increasing, since . Phase invariance of real sphere measure makes the average of equal to . All parameter derivatives pass through this compact smooth integral. Thus is nonnegative and increasing. Real flux gives

For general , radial smoothings are smooth plurisubharmonic on smaller domains. Their positive Laplacians converge distributionally. The preceding cutoff argument gives mass convergence at every radius without boundary mass. In any fixed larger compact ball only countably many spheres have positive mass: for each integer , only finitely many disjoint spheres can have mass at least . Their countable union includes every positive mass sphere.

Pass the smooth monotonicity inequality at two radii outside this countable set. Approach any desired positive radii from below by such radii, keeping their order. These choices exist because a countable set has Lebesgue measure zero while each nonempty interval has positive measure. Increasing open balls exhaust the desired open ball, so continuity from below and the continuous positive denominator prove the inequality at every radius. A fixed larger interior ball has finite mass and bounds all smaller densities. Hence the nonnegative increasing function has a finite limit at zero, its infimum.

Its integral over disjoint intervals is bounded by this common bound times their total length, which proves absolute continuity there. We subtracted finite sphere means, not a possibly infinite center value.

Solutions

Solution 1. Proposition 3.2 gives subharmonicity. Polar integration and integration by parts give The endpoint term tends to zero, for example by the logarithmic bound from the scalar foundations. Thus the limit and its canonical representative are zero. At every nonzero point the sequence tends to zero, while at zero it remains minus infinity. The limsup inequality holds everywhere and equality fails only on that null singleton.

Solution 2. Every term is harmonic on each component and bounded above by zero. It does not collapse on any compact in the first disk. On a positive-area compact disk in the second, its norm is , unbounded along every subsequence. An -convergent sequence has bounded norms by the triangle inequality, so no local subsequence exists. This is precisely where connected propagation is needed.

Solution 3. The real part of the holomorphic term has zero Levi form. Direct differentiation of the remaining quadratic gives Thus the smooth function is real subharmonic and has diagonal Levi entries . For , however, . Its line Laplacian is , so it fails the line criterion.

Solution 4. Both nonzero polynomial logarithms are proper plurisubharmonic by Proposition 3.2; their maximum is so by Proposition 1.2. Their common zero is only the origin: and force both coordinates to vanish. The exponential of their maximum is homogeneous of degree two under positive real dilation, so Proposition 4.3 gives . Since , Continuity from above of this finite local measure as gives zero mass to the origin. A singular function value need not give a Laplacian atom in real dimension four.

Thus the open-ball Laplacian mass lies between and . No regularity of the zero hypersurface was assumed.

Proposition 6.2 with therefore gives, on , , the density For the sine value, the scalar angle-addition identities give at , while . Thus and the positive sine is . Solution 8. Substitute in Proposition 6.1 with . Only the real rays contribute. Multiplication by two gives the density there. At each finite endpoint the function and gradient have the square-root bounds proved in Proposition 6.1, so the small-circle Green terms vanish and there are no endpoint atoms. The two rays contribute equally: The antiderivative follows directly by differentiation on and its zero limit at . At the mass is .

Programme proof locations and freely accessible sources

  • Positive derivatives and canonical representatives, Lemma 2.1, Theorems 3.1–3.2 and Corollary 3.3: complete shell formula, canonical representative, local integrability, sphere recovery and radial smoothing.
  • Order, positivity and distributional limits, Corollary 3.3 and Theorems 4.1, 5.1–5.2: Radon measures, sequential bounded-test convergence, and convergence on continuous compact tests. Convolution as addition of supports, B1–B3 and Proposition 5.1: parameter tests and local smoothing.
  • Boundary flux and weak identities, Theorem 2.1 and Corollaries 2.2–2.4: flux, Green identities and planar corners. Point sources and complex Gaussian kernels, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2: normalized Laplacian and log-modulus sources, with local logarithm proof.
  • Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones, polydisk Cauchy proof, (3.1), and Lemma 3.1: locally convergent power series with coefficient and derivative bounds, and the identity principle.
  • Integration foundations, §§15–16; scalar foundations, §§12–13; finite algebra, §§10.1–10.6; and angular foundations, A4–A5: the measure, compactness, scalar calculus, Euclidean and sphere proofs used above.
  • Ahmed Zeriahi, Introduction to Pluripotential Theory, SEAMS School, Hanoi, 2017, free author-hosted lecture notes, Proposition 1.34, Propositions 1.45–1.46, Theorem 1.49, Lemma 2.26, Theorem 2.32 and Corollary 2.34.
